title: Trigonometric Function
body:
$\sin$, $\cos$, $\tan$, and their reciprocals ($\csc$, $\sec$, $\cot$) and inverses ($\arcsin$,
$\arccos$, $\arctan$). Defined by ratios in a right triangle, but for calculus the useful picture
is the **unit circle**: $(\cos\theta, \sin\theta)$ is the point at angle $\theta$, which is why
they are periodic and why $\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1$ is just Pythagoras.

In calculus they are the standard example of a function that is **not** algebraic (transcendental),
and they are the reason radians exist: $\frac{d}{dx}\sin x = \cos x$ only holds in radians. In
degrees it picks up a factor of $\pi/180$ and every formula in the course gets uglier.

## Derivatives cycle with period four

$$
\sin x \;\to\; \cos x \;\to\; -\sin x \;\to\; -\cos x \;\to\; \sin x
$$

The ones starting with **c** pick up the minus sign: $(\cos x)' = -\sin x$, $(\csc x)' = -\csc x
\cot x$, $(\cot x)' = -\csc^2 x$. All of it descends from one [[Limit]]:

$$
\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{\sin x}{x} = 1
$$

## Identities worth keeping

- $\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1$, and its two derived forms $\tan^2 + 1 = \sec^2$,
  $1 + \cot^2 = \csc^2$
- double angle: $\sin 2\theta = 2\sin\theta\cos\theta$, $\cos 2\theta = \cos^2\theta - \sin^2\theta$
- the half-angle forms of $\cos 2\theta$, which are how you integrate $\sin^2$ and $\cos^2$ at all

## Where else they turn up

- [[Polar Form]] in [[LINEAR ALGEBRA]]: $z = r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta) = re^{i\theta}$.
  Multiplying complex numbers adds arguments, so trig is what rotation is made of, and Euler's
  formula is the statement that the trig functions and the exponential are the same object seen
  from two sides.
- [[Integration By Trigonometric Substitution]] in [[CALCULUS 2]]: the Pythagorean identity run
  backwards, to turn $\sqrt{1-x^2}$ into something without a root. [[Trigonometric Integrals]] is
  what that substitution hands you, and [[Polar Coordinates]] is where the identities get used on
  the region rather than the integrand.
- [[FOURIER AND COMPLEX ANALYSIS]]: sines and cosines as an
  [[Orthogonal Functions|orthogonal basis]] rather than as a family of formulas, and
  [[Fourier Series]] as the expansion of an arbitrary function in that basis.
